question:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine, will the 1-incidence rate ratio overestimate / underestimate / correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy?

Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of vaccinees is completely protected for the whole follow up and a fraction 1-p is phenotypically identical to unvaccinated.

With constant unvaccinated hazard λ0

S_u(t)=exp(-λ0t)

S_v(t)=p·1+(1-p)S_u(t)

Risk_v(T)=1-S_v(T)=(1-p)[1-S_u(T)]
Risk_u(T)=1-S_u(T)

Hence Risk_v/Risk_u =1-p for all T, so 1–risk ratio =p, the proportion completely protected.

The rate that is actually used is

h_v(t)= -S_v′/S_v = λ0 (1-p)S_u(t)/[p+(1-p)S_u(t)]

h_v(t)<λ0(1-p) and h_v(t) decreases with t. The person-time rate in the vaccinated arm is

IR_v = Cases_v / PT_v = (1-p)[1-S_u]/[pT+(1-p)∫0^T S_u]

IR_u = [1-S_u]/∫0^T S_u

so that

IRR = IR_v/IR_u = (1-p)∫ S_u/[pT+(1-p)∫ S_u]
     = (1-p)/[1+ pT/∫ S_u –p] < 1-p

because T/∫0^T S_u >1. Hence

1–IRR =1-(1-p)/[1+ pT/∫ S_u –p] >p.

The protected individuals contribute person-time but never cases, so the vaccinated incidence rate is driven down more than the true per-exposure risk reduction in the susceptible 1-p fraction. In the limit the cumulative-risk-based efficacy 1–RR =p is the proportion protected, i.e. the true per-exposure efficacy, whereas 1–IRR is inflated. In particular for a leaky vaccine the rate ratio is unbiased for per-exposure efficacy, whereas for an all-or-nothing vaccine the rate ratio overestimates it and the bias increases with follow-up time.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing product a fraction f of vaccinees is made completely
impervious to infection and the remaining 1–f is left with the same hazard
per contact as an unvaccinated person.  With constant exposure rate r and
per-contact attack probability p, q = 1–p

Unvaccinated
N(t)=N0 q^{rt}          Events(T)=N0[1–q^{rT}]
PT_unv = N0[1–q^{rT}]/[–r ln q]
IR_u = Events/PT_unv = –r ln q  i.e. constant in T.

Vaccinated all-or-nothing
N_v(t)=N0[ f + (1–f)q^{rt}]
Events_v(T)=N0(1–f)[1–q^{rT}]
PT_v = N0{ f T + (1–f)[1–q^{rT}]/[–r ln q] }
IR_v(T)= (1–f)[1–q^{rT}]/[ f T –r⁻¹ln q⁻¹⁻¹? ] 
IR_v / IR_u = (1–f)[1–q^{rT}] /[ –r ln q f T + (1–f)[1–q^{rT}] ].

Hence
IR_v/IR_u = 1–f  at T≈0 and IR_v/IR_u ↓ 0 as T→∞
so that 1–IR_v/IR_u  starts at the true average per-exposure efficacy
VE_pe = f and then increases with duration of follow-up.

In the limit of very short follow-up or for a single-exposure / risk ratio
construction,
1–RRcum = 1–IRR0 ≃ f,
i.e. the proportion completely protected, which is the usual
convention for vaccine efficacy against infection.  Averaged over the
usual finite, and particularly longer, follow-up the protected
fraction contributes person-time without events while the susceptible
fraction is depleted in the unvaccinated arm, the observed incidence
density in the vaccine arm falls with time and the empirical
1–IR_v/IR_u is >f.  It is in this usual incidence-rate sense that
1–incidence rate ratio overestimates the true per-contact, i.e. the
hazard per exposure, efficacy of an all-or-nothing vaccine; the bias
vanishes for essentially acute, short follow-up where the risk ratio
and the rate ratio coincide and is often quoted as the ‘correct’
estimate of the proportion protected f.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. underestimate

In an all-or-nothing model the vaccine gives complete protection to a fraction of recipients and no protection at all to the remainder. The per-exposure efficacy that is of biological interest is the efficacy conditional on being in the protected subset, i.e. essentially 100% protection per exposure for those individuals.

The incidence rate ratio 1 – IRR is a population-average measure over the whole vaccinated cohort and over the whole follow-up period. It pools the completely protected fraction with the unprotected fraction who continue to accrue infections at the same rate per exposure as unvaccinated subjects. Because the denominator includes person-time contributed by both protected and unprotected vaccinated persons, the observed incidence reduction is diluted by the ongoing risk in the unprotected sub-group.

As a result the average reduction captured by 1 – IRR is smaller than the true per-exposure protection experienced by the individuals who are actually rendered immune. In other words the incidence rate based estimate is a diluted population average and will underestimate the per-exposure efficacy that would be seen if one could condition on the truly protected individuals.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. The standard definition of vaccine efficacy against infection is 1 minus the incidence rate ratio, which compares the instantaneous hazard of infection in vaccinated versus unvaccinated persons. For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of recipients is completely protected with hazard 0 and the remaining 1-p is effectively unvaccinated with the baseline hazard λ0. The average hazard in the vaccinated arm is therefore (1-p) λ0 at any point in follow-up, so the hazard ratio is constant at 1-p. Hence 1 – IRR = p, which is exactly the proportion of recipients who are made non-susceptible and the reduction in risk per exposure. Under this model the incidence rate ratio tracks the per-exposure effect without systematic bias.

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of recipients is completely protected and hazard =0 and a fraction 1-p is completely unprotected and has the unvaccinated hazard λ0. 

Cumulative risk
V(t) = (1-p)[1-exp(-λ0 t)] 
U(t) = 1-exp(-λ0 t)
so that 
RR(t)=V/U = 1-p

is constant in time. The per-exposure / individual efficacy is
VE0 = 1-RR = p.

Instantaneous hazard in the vaccinated cohort is

hV(t)= λ0 (1-p) e^{-λ0t} / [p+(1-p)e^{-λ0t} ]

so that the instantaneous hazard ratio is

HR(t)= (1-p) e^{-λ0t} / [p+(1-p)e^{-λ0t}] ≤ 1-p

with equality only at t =0. HR(t) falls with follow-up because protected individuals accumulate immortal person-time while the unprotected susceptible are depleted by infection. The incidence rate ratio observed over a finite follow-up is the time-averaged HR(t) < 1-p. Hence

1 - IRRobs = 1 - <HR(t)> > 1-(1-p)=p = VEper-exposure

i.e. the usual 1 - incidence rate ratio gives a time-averaged efficacy that is larger than the true all-or-nothing, per-exposure efficacy p and increases with duration of follow-up. The risk ratio, not the rate ratio, is the constant estimator for an all-or-nothing effect; the rate ratio is the appropriate constant estimator for a leaky, per-exposure effect.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For a leaky vaccine the hazard per unit exposure is reduced by the same factor in every vaccinee so that

VEleaky = 1 – λV/λU = 1 – IRR

is the reduction in risk per exposure. 

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of vaccinees is made completely immune and a fraction 1-p remains completely susceptible.  Conditional on being susceptible the force of infection is

λV|susc = λU ,

i.e. the true per-exposure efficacy in a susceptible vaccinee is

VEpexp|susc = 1 – λV|susc/λU = 0 .

At the population level the whole-cohort hazard is

λV = (1-p)λU ,

so that

IRR = λV/λU = 1-p

and

1 – IRR = p

is the proportion of the cohort that is completely protected, the usual all-or-nothing population vaccine efficacy.  The incidence density ratio therefore reflects the reduction in the number of susceptible hosts and not a reduction in the risk per exposure in those who remain susceptible.  In the textbook limit the per-exposure efficacy is nil for the susceptible fraction, whereas 1–IRR = p > 0 , i.e. the incidence rate ratio gives a positive population efficacy where the biologically relevant per-exposure efficacy is zero.  In that sense the conventional 1–IRR estimate is an upward, i.e. optimistic, estimate of the true per-exposure protection; the same population number is the usual all-or-nothing efficacy ~ the proportion protected, which is <100 % and therefore underestimates the 100 % protection that is experienced by the p fraction that is actually protected.

15.text:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine the population can be written as a mixture

* a fraction $\pi$ is completely immune, $h_{v|{\rm prot}}=0$, 
* a fraction $1-\pi$ is unprotected and has the same per-exposure risk as an unvaccinated subject, $h_{v|{\rm unprot}}=h_{u}$.

Hence for a constant per-exposure risk

$S_{v}(t)=\pi+(1-\pi)S_{u}(t)$

and the hazard in the vaccinated who are still at risk is

$h_{v}(t)= -\frac{S_{v}'(t)}{S_{v}(t)}
      =\frac{(1-\pi)S_{u}(t)h_{u}(t)}{\pi+(1-\pi)S_{u}(t)}$

so that the instantaneous hazard ratio is

$\displaystyle{\rm HR}(t)=\frac{h_{v}(t)}{h_{u}(t)}
      =\frac{(1-\pi)S_{u}(t)}{\pi+(1-\pi)S_{u}(t)}$

$\rm HR(0)=1-\pi$ and $\rm HR(t)$ is monotone decreasing to $0$ with time as the susceptible vaccinated are depleted.  The per-exposure, i.e. individual-level, efficacy is

${\rm VE}_{pe}=1-\frac{r_{v}}{r_{u}}= \pi$,

with $r$ the risk per exposure. The cumulative risk ratio is in fact time-constant,

$C_{v}(t)=(1-\pi)C_{u}(t)\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;RR(t)=1-\pi$,

so $1-RR$ recovers $\pi$. The person-time incidence rate is an average of $h_{v}(t)/h_{u}(t)$ over the follow-up. Because $HR(t)<1-\pi$ for $t>0$ the time-averaged
$\overline{HR}= {\rm IRR}<1-\pi$. Hence

$1-{\rm IRR}>1-(1-\pi)=\pi={\rm VE}_{pe},$

i.e. $1-$ incidence rate ratio is upwardly biased for the true per-exposure efficacy. In the limit of short follow-up $\rm IRR\to1-\pi$ and the bias disappears; with usual follow-up the $1-\rm IRR$ estimate overstates the per-exposure effect. This is the classic all-or-nothing vs leaky distinction; the $1-\rm IRR$ is unbiased for a leaky vaccine.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For an instantaneous exposure the hazard for a vaccinated person who remains
uninfected is

h_v(t)=λ0 ×  S_v(t) / [π+ S_v(t) ]

where λ0 is the unvaccinated per-exposure hazard, π is the fraction that is
completely protected in an all-or-nothing model and S_v(t)=(1−π)exp(−λ0t) is
the fraction of the vaccinated cohort still susceptible at t. Hence

HR(t)=h_v(t)/h0(t)= [1−π]exp(−λ0t) / [π+(1−π)exp(−λ0t)] ,

which is decreasing in t from HR(0)=1−π to 0. The per-exposure, i.e. the
initial, efficacy is

VE_pe =1−HR(0)=π .

The usual 1−IRR is the time-averaged hazard ratio over the follow-up.
With person-time denominator

IRR(T)= (1−π)[1−e^{−λ0T}] / [πλ0T+(1−π)[1−e^{−λ0T}] ] <1−π

for T>0, so that

1−IRR(T)= πλ0T / [πλ0T+(1−π)[1−e^{−λ0T}]] >π =VE_pe,

with equality only in the rare-disease / short follow-up limit λ0T≪1.
In other words the protected fraction contributes person-time but never
infections, the remaining susceptible vaccinated are progressively depleted
by infection, and the average incidence rate in the vaccinated arm is
diluted below the instantaneous per-exposure rate. The time averaged
1−IRR therefore is larger than the true per-exposure protection π, i.e.
it overestimates per-exposure vaccine efficacy for an all-or-nothing
vaccine. In the instantaneous rare-event limit the two coincide.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of vaccinees is completely protected and a fraction 1-p remains fully susceptible with the same per-exposure risk μ0 as unvaccinated.

Per exposure
Risk_v = (1-p) μ0
VE_pe = 1 - Risk_v/Risk_u = 1 – (1-p) = p

With constant exposure rate e, λ0 = e μ0 is the infection rate in unvaccinated.
At time t the surviving vaccinated cohort is
S_v(t)= p + (1-p) e^{-λ0 t}
so that
hazard_v(t)= λ0 (1-p) e^{-λ0 t} / [p+(1-p)e^{-λ0 t}]

The instantaneous hazard ratio is 1-p at t=0 and declines thereafter, i.e. hazards are non-proportional. The observable incidence-rate ratio over a finite follow up T is

IRR(T)= [N_v/PT_v]/[N_u/PT_u]
      = (1-p)(1-e^{-λ0 T}) / [(1-p)(1-e^{-λ0 T})+ p λ0 T] < 1-p

with IRR → 1-p as T→0 and IRR →0 as T→∞. Hence

1-IRR(T) > 1-(1-p)=p = VE_pe

The person-time denominator is inflated by the permanently immune fraction p that continues to contribute time at risk without events. The average hazard ratio over follow-up is therefore smaller than the true per-exposure hazard ratio at time zero, so the naive 1-incidence rate ratio is an upwardly biased estimate of the population average per-exposure efficacy. The cumulative incidence ratio stays at 1-p, i.e. it estimates the all-or-nothing efficacy p correctly.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the population of vaccinees is effectively a mixture of fully protected individuals and fully susceptible individuals who experience the same per-exposure hazard as unvaccinated. If a fraction p is completely protected, the incidence rate in the vaccinated group is (1-p) times the incidence rate in the unvaccinated group at any time, so the hazard ratio is constant and equal to HR = 1-p. Hence 1 - IRR = p. That p is both the proportion of individuals who are rendered immune and the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated cohort, so the incidence rate ratio maps directly to the per-exposure efficacy under the all-or-nothing mechanism. In practice the IRR is the usual estimator for VE and remains unbiased for the per-exposure effect in this model.

every vaccinated person

λ1(t)=λ0(t)[1-VEe]    →    IRR = λ1/λ0 = 1-VEe

so that

VEIRR =1-IRR

is the usual per-exposure/hazard VE.

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of recipients is made
completely immune and the remaining fraction s=1-p remains biologically
identical to an unvaccinated person. On the population level

λ1(t)= s λ0(t)  ,

so that

IRR = s =1-p ,      VEIRR =1-IRR =p ,

i.e. the rate ratio returns the proportion of recipients who are
completely protected, the all-or-nothing, per-person VE.  For the
s=1-p persons who remain susceptible the biological risk per exposure is
unchanged, the true per-exposure/hazard reduction conditional on being
susceptible is VEe|s =0.  In that mechanistic sense the rate-ratio
estimate VEIRR =p>0 is an upwardly biased estimate of the per-exposure
reduction experienced by a susceptible vaccinated individual.  In the
average-population sense VEIRR is the proportion protected and is often
quoted as the all-or-nothing VE, which is the quantity that is
over-estimated if one interprets it as a genuine per-exposure hazard
reduction for everyone.  This is the usual over-estimation of a leaky
per-exposure efficacy by 1-IRR when the true mechanism is all-or-nothing.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of vaccinees is completely protected and a fraction 1-p is completely unprotected. With a constant force of infection λ0 the instantaneous hazard in the unvaccinated is λ0 and the instantaneous hazard in a newly vaccinated cohort is

hV(0) = (1-p) λ0

so that the true per-exposure, per-contact efficacy is

VEpe = 1 – hV(0)/λ0 = p

and the instantaneous rate ratio is 1-p at time 0.

With follow-up the unprotected vaccinees are depleted by infection whereas the protected vaccinees accumulate person-time at risk with zero events. The person-time denominator of the vaccinated group therefore becomes progressively enriched with protected susceptibles. The average incidence rate over a finite follow-up t is

RateV(t) = [(1-p)(1−e^{−λ0 t})] / [p t + (1-p)(1−e^{−λ0 t})/λ0] .

Hence

IRR(t)= RateV(t)/λ0 = (1-p)(1−e^{−λ0 t}) / [p λ0 t + (1-p)(1−e^{−λ0 t})] < 1-p

for t>0, with IRR(t)→0 as t→∞. 1−IRR(t) therefore starts at p and increases with time, i.e. the rate-ratio based estimate 1−IRR > p = VEpe.

In the limit the cumulative risk ratio remains

RRcum = (1-p)[1−e^{−λ0 t}] / [1−e^{−λ0 t}] =1-p,

so the cumulative-risk ratio estimates the all-or-nothing efficacy correctly, whereas the incidence rate ratio is progressively biased downwards and 1−IRR progressively overestimates the true per-exposure efficacy. This is the classic depletion-of-susceptibles bias for an all-or-nothing vaccine; the bias is absent for a leaky vaccine where IRR=1−VEpe is constant in time.

The average hazard in the vaccinated arm is therefore (1-p) λ0 at any point in follow-up, so the hazard ratio is constant at 1-p. Hence 1 – IRR = p, which is exactly the proportion of recipients who are made non-susceptible and the reduction in risk per exposure. Under this model the incidence rate ratio tracks the per-exposure effect without systematic bias.

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the population can be written as a mixture

* a fraction $\pi$ is completely immune, $h_{v|{\rm prot}}=0$, 
* a fraction $1-\pi$ is unprotected and has the same per-exposure risk as an unvaccinated subject, $h_{v|{\rm unprot}}=h_{u}$.

Hence for a constant per-exposure risk

$S_{v}(t)=\pi+(1-\pi)S_{u}(t)$

and the hazard in the vaccinated who are still at risk is

$h_{v}(t)= -\frac{S_{v}'(t)}{S_{v}(t)}
      =\frac{(1-\pi)S_{u}(t)h_{u}(t)}{\pi+(1-\pi)S_{u}(t)}$

so that the instantaneous hazard ratio is

$\displaystyle{\rm HR}(t)=\frac{h_{v}(t)}{h_{u}(t)}
      =\frac{(1-\pi)S_{u}(t)}{\pi+(1-\pi)S_{u}(t)}$

$\rm HR(0)=1-\pi$ and $\rm HR(t)$ is monotone decreasing to $0$ with time as the susceptible vaccinated are depleted.  The per-exposure, i.e. individual-level, efficacy is

${\rm VE}_{pe}=1-\frac{r_{v}}{r_{u}}= \pi$,

with $r$ the risk per exposure. The cumulative risk ratio is in fact time-constant,

$C_{v}(t)=(1-\pi)C_{u}(t)\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;RR(t)=1-\pi$,

so $1-RR$ recovers $\pi$. The person-time incidence rate is an average of $h_{v}(t)/h_{u}(t)$ over the follow-up. Because $HR(t)<1-\pi$ for $t>0$ the time-averaged
$\overline{HR}= {\rm IRR}<1-\pi$. Hence

$1-{\rm IRR}>1-(1-\pi)=\pi={\rm VE}_{pe},$

i.e. $1-$ incidence rate ratio is upwardly biased for the true per-exposure efficacy. In the limit of short follow-up $\rm IRR\to1-\pi$ and the bias disappears; with usual follow-up the $1-\rm IRR$ estimate overstates the per-exposure effect. This is the classic all-or-nothing vs leaky distinction; the $1-\rm IRR$ is unbiased for a leaky vaccine.

HR(t)=h_v(t)/h0(t)= [1−π]exp(−λ0t) / [π+(1−π)exp(−λ0t)] ,

which is decreasing in t from HR(0)=1−π to 0. The per-exposure, i.e. the
initial, efficacy is

VE_pe =1−HR(0)=π .

The usual 1−IRR is the time-averaged hazard ratio over the follow-up.
With person-time denominator

IRR(T)= (1−π)[1−e^{−λ0T}] / [πλ0T+(1−π)[1−e^{−λ0T}] ] <1−π

for T>0, so that

1−IRR(T)= πλ0T / [πλ0T+(1−π)[1−e^{−λ0T}]] >π =VE_pe,

with equality only in the rare-disease / short follow-up limit λ0T≪1.

infections, the remaining susceptible vaccinated are progressively depleted
by infection, and the average incidence rate in the vaccinated arm is
diluted below the instantaneous per-exposure rate. The time averaged
1−IRR therefore is larger than the true per-exposure protection π, i.e.
it overestimates per-exposure vaccine efficacy for an all-or-nothing
vaccine. In the instantaneous rare-event limit the two coincide.

C. correctly estimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the population of vaccinees is effectively a mixture of fully protected individuals and fully susceptible individuals who experience the same per-exposure hazard as unvaccinated. A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction p of vaccinees is completely protected and a fraction 1-p is completely unprotected. With a constant force of infection λ0 the instantaneous hazard in the unvaccinated is λ0 and the instantaneous hazard in a newly vaccinated cohort is

hV(0) = (1-p) λ0

so that the true per-exposure, per-contact efficacy is

VEpe = 1 – hV(0)/λ0 = p

and the instantaneous rate ratio is 1-p at time 0.

With follow-up the unprotected vaccinees are depleted by infection whereas the protected vaccinees accumulate person-time at risk with zero events. The person-time denominator of the vaccinated group therefore becomes progressively enriched with protected susceptibles. The average incidence rate over a finite follow-up t is

Hence

IRR(t)= RateV(t)/λ0 = (1-p)(1−e^{−λ0 t}) / [p λ0 t + (1-p)(1−e^{−λ0 t})] < 1-p

for t>0, with IRR(t)→0 as t→∞. 1−IRR(t) therefore starts at p and increases with time, i.e. the rate-ratio based estimate 1−IRR > p = VEpe.

In the limit the cumulative risk ratio remains

RRcum = (1-p)[1−e^{−λ0 t}] / [1−e^{−λ0 t}] =1-p,

so the cumulative-risk ratio estimates the all-or-nothing efficacy correctly, whereas the incidence rate ratio is progressively biased downwards and 1−IRR progressively overestimates the true per-exposure efficacy. 7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the confusion here is really about which hazard we are talking about, and the definition of “per-exposure” efficacy for an all-or-nothing product.

If a fraction p is made completely non-susceptible and the remaining 1-p is biologically identical to unvaccinated, the population-level force of infection in the vaccinated arm is at any calendar time

h_v^pop(t) = (1-p) h_0(t) + p·0 = (1-p) h_0(t).

That is the average hazard per vaccinated person, including the p who are immune. The total number of events in the arm is (1-p) times what you would get in an unvaccinated arm with the same size, and the total person-time contributed by the arm is the same person-time as an unvaccinated arm. So

IR_v = (1-p) IR_u ,   IRR = 1-p ,   1-IRR = p

at every point in follow-up, under the usual proportional-hazards definition of VE = 1 - hazard ratio.

The time-varying expression

h_v(t)=h_0(t)(1-p)S_0(t)/[p+(1-p)S_0(t)]

that is being quoted is the hazard conditional on still being uninfected at time t. It conditions on survival and therefore on the depletion of the 1-p susceptible fraction. It is the hazard among the selected sub-cohort that remains at risk, not the average hazard per randomly chosen vaccinee at time t. Conditioning on survival creates the apparent decline to zero: the survivors become increasingly enriched with the permanently immune. That is a selection effect, not a change in the per-exposure risk for a vaccinee who is susceptible.

Per-exposure efficacy is defined as the reduction in risk per exposure on average in the vaccinated cohort, i.e. 1 - h_v^pop / h_0. That quantity is constant and equal to p. The cumulative risk ratio is also 1-p, and the incidence rate ratio tracks it. In the rare-disease/short follow-up limit the conditional hazard coincides with the population hazard, which is why the two are usually written as the same in practice.

So the 1 - incidence rate ratio is not an upwardly biased estimate of per-exposure efficacy; it is the population-average per-exposure efficacy itself. The “overestimate” argument is an overestimate of the overestimate, i.e. it mistakes the hazard among survivors for the hazard per exposure in the cohort. That is the same point made by Colleagues 13 and 14: for an all-or-nothing mechanism the IRR is a constant estimator of the proportion protected, which is exactly how per-exposure VE is conventionally defined.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

The per-exposure quantity that is normally quoted for an all-or-nothing product is the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated cohort, not the hazard conditional on remaining susceptible at time t.

Write the vaccinated cohort as a mixture. A fraction p is made completely immune, hazard = 0 for all t. A fraction 1-p is biologically identical to an unvaccinated subject, hazard = h0(t) per exposure. The marginal population hazard in the vaccinated arm is therefore

hV(t)= p·0 + (1-p)·h0(t)= (1-p) h0(t)

at every instant, i.e. the average hazard per exposure in a randomly sampled vaccinee is a constant fraction of the unvaccinated hazard. Hence

HR(t)=hV(t)/h0(t)=1-p ,      VEpe =1-HR = p

for all t. The incidence density is proportional to hazard per exposure times the exposure rate, so the incidence rate ratio is

IRR = IRV/IRU = (1-p)h0/h0 =1-p

and 1-IRR = p. That p is both the proportion of recipients who are rendered non-susceptible and the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated population. 

The decreasing expression HR(t)=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0] that is quoted for the overestimate case is the hazard conditional on being still uninfected at time t, i.e. the hazard in the residual susceptible pool after depletion of the unprotected fraction by infection. That conditional hazard is indeed falling with follow-up because the cohort becomes progressively enriched with the permanently immune fraction. It is a selection effect, not a change in the per-exposure risk for an individual who remains susceptible. 

The cumulative risk ratio is constant, RR(t)=V(t)/U(t)=1-p, and the incidence rate ratio is constant for the same mixture reason. In the usual rare-disease/ short follow-up limit the time-averaged rate ratio coincides with the instantaneous ratio, and with the mixture definition there is no systematic bias: 1-IRR estimates the proportion protected, which is the conventional definition of per-exposure efficacy for an all-or-nothing vaccine. The “inflation” of 1-IRR is the well-known difference between a conditional hazard in the residual susceptible and the unconditional average hazard per exposure, not a bias of the rate ratio for the population per-exposure effect.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

The point that keeps recurring in the A arguments is the time-dependent hazard among survivors

h_v(t)=h0(t) (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]

and the claim that the time-averaged incidence density ratio is therefore <1-p. That conditional hazard is the hazard of remaining uninfected vaccinees, i.e. it is conditioned on survival to t. It is not the marginal hazard per exposure opportunity.

Per-exposure vaccine efficacy is defined as the reduction in the hazard of infection per exposure opportunity. For an all-or-nothing product the exposure process is a mixture:

* fraction p has hazard 0 for all t,
* fraction 1-p has hazard h0(t) for all t, identical to unvaccinated.

Hence the marginal population hazard in the vaccinated arm is

h_v^M(t)= p×0 + (1-p) h0(t)= (1-p) h0(t)

at every t, and the marginal hazard ratio

HR^M(t)=h_v^M(t)/h0(t)=1-p

is constant. The total expected events in follow-up T are

E_v(T)= (1-p) N ∫0^T h0(u) du

and total person-time is N T, because person-time is accumulated by the whole vaccinated cohort, protected and unprotected alike. The incidence rate is therefore

IR_v = E_v / N T = (1-p) × [∫0^T h0(u) du / T] .

The unvaccinated rate is IR_u = [∫0^T h0(u) du / T]. So

IRR = IR_v/IR_u =1-p

for any T>0, and 1-IRR = p. The p we obtain is both the proportion of recipients made non-susceptible and the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated cohort. That is the usual epidemiologic definition of VE =1-IRR.

The decreasing HR(t) quoted by colleagues 1,10,11, etc. is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected, h_v(t)= -S_v'/S_v. It declines because the susceptible 1-p fraction is progressively depleted by infection while the p fraction remains and inflates the denominator S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t). That is a selection effect among survivors, not a change in the biological per-exposure risk. It is exactly why the cumulative risk ratio

RR_cum(T)=[1-S_v(T)]/[1-S0(T)]=1-p

is constant, and why in the rare-disease/short follow-up limit the conditional and marginal hazards coincide.

If 1-IRR were truly >p, VE would tend to 1 as follow-up lengthened, which would be a cumulative protection statement about the depletion of the susceptible pool, not a statement about the biological risk per exposure. The operational VE used in trials is the marginal 1-IRR, which for an all-or-nothing mechanism is the proportion protected p, i.e. the per-exposure efficacy by the standard definition. This is the same reasoning given by colleagues 13 and 14, and it is why the risk ratio and the rate ratio are both 1-p for the marginal quantity of interest.

I think the confusion here is really about which hazard we are talking about, and the definition of “per-exposure” efficacy for an all-or-nothing product.

If a fraction p is made completely non-susceptible and the remaining 1-p is biologically identical to unvaccinated, the population-level force of infection in the vaccinated arm is at any calendar time

h_v^pop(t) = (1-p) h_0(t) + p·0 = (1-p) h_0(t).

That is the average hazard per vaccinated person, including the p who are immune. The total number of events in the arm is (1-p) times what you would get in an unvaccinated arm with the same size, and the total person-time contributed by the arm is the same person-time as an unvaccinated arm. So

IR_v = (1-p) IR_u ,   IRR = 1-p ,   1-IRR = p

at every point in follow-up, under the usual proportional-hazards definition of VE = 1 - hazard ratio.

The time-varying expression

h_v(t)=h_0(t)(1-p)S_0(t)/[p+(1-p)S_0(t)]

that is being quoted is the hazard conditional on still being uninfected at time t. It conditions on survival and therefore on the depletion of the 1-p susceptible fraction. It is the hazard among the selected sub-cohort that remains at risk, not the average hazard per randomly chosen vaccinee at time t. Conditioning on survival creates the apparent decline to zero: the survivors become increasingly enriched with the permanently immune. That is a selection effect, not a change in the per-exposure risk for a vaccinee who is susceptible.

Per-exposure efficacy is defined as the reduction in risk per exposure on average in the vaccinated cohort, i.e. 1 - h_v^pop / h_0. That quantity is constant and equal to p. The cumulative risk ratio is also 1-p, and the incidence rate ratio tracks it. In the rare-disease/short follow-up limit the conditional hazard coincides with the population hazard, which is why the two are usually written as the same in practice.

So the 1 - incidence rate ratio is not an upwardly biased estimate of per-exposure efficacy; it is the population-average per-exposure efficacy itself. The “overestimate” argument is an overestimate of the overestimate, i.e. it mistakes the hazard among survivors for the hazard per exposure in the cohort. That is the same point made by Colleagues 13 and 14: for an all-or-nothing mechanism the IRR is a constant estimator of the proportion protected, which is exactly how per-exposure VE is conventionally defined.

C. correctly estimate

The per-exposure quantity that is normally quoted for an all-or-nothing product is the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated cohort, not the hazard conditional on remaining susceptible at time t.

Write the vaccinated cohort as a mixture. A fraction p is made completely immune, hazard = 0 for all t. A fraction 1-p is biologically identical to an unvaccinated subject, hazard = h0(t) per exposure. The marginal population hazard in the vaccinated arm is therefore

hV(t)= p·0 + (1-p)·h0(t)= (1-p) h0(t)

at every instant, i.e. the average hazard per exposure in a randomly sampled vaccinee is a constant fraction of the unvaccinated hazard. Hence

HR(t)=hV(t)/h0(t)=1-p ,      VEpe =1-HR = p

for all t. The incidence density is proportional to hazard per exposure times the exposure rate, so the incidence rate ratio is

IRR = IRV/IRU = (1-p)h0/h0 =1-p

and 1-IRR = p. That p is both the proportion of recipients who are rendered non-susceptible and the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated population. 

The decreasing expression HR(t)=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0] that is quoted for the overestimate case is the hazard conditional on being still uninfected at time t, i.e. the hazard in the residual susceptible pool after depletion of the unprotected fraction by infection. That conditional hazard is indeed falling with follow-up because the cohort becomes progressively enriched with the permanently immune fraction. It is a selection effect, not a change in the per-exposure risk for an individual who remains susceptible. 

The cumulative risk ratio is constant, RR(t)=V(t)/U(t)=1-p, and the incidence rate ratio is constant for the same mixture reason. In the usual rare-disease/ short follow-up limit the time-averaged rate ratio coincides with the instantaneous ratio, and with the mixture definition there is no systematic bias: 1-IRR estimates the proportion protected, which is the conventional definition of per-exposure efficacy for an all-or-nothing vaccine. The “inflation” of 1-IRR is the well-known difference between a conditional hazard in the residual susceptible and the unconditional average hazard per exposure, not a bias of the rate ratio for the population per-exposure effect.

C. correctly estimate

The point that keeps recurring in the A arguments is the time-dependent hazard among survivors

h_v(t)=h0(t) (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]

and the claim that the time-averaged incidence density ratio is therefore <1-p. That conditional hazard is the hazard of remaining uninfected vaccinees, i.e. it is conditioned on survival to t. It is not the marginal hazard per exposure opportunity.

Per-exposure vaccine efficacy is defined as the reduction in the hazard of infection per exposure opportunity. For an all-or-nothing product the exposure process is a mixture:

* fraction p has hazard 0 for all t,
* fraction 1-p has hazard h0(t) for all t, identical to unvaccinated.

Hence the marginal population hazard in the vaccinated arm is

h_v^M(t)= p×0 + (1-p) h0(t)= (1-p) h0(t)

at every t, and the marginal hazard ratio

HR^M(t)=h_v^M(t)/h0(t)=1-p

is constant. The total expected events in follow-up T are

E_v(T)= (1-p) N ∫0^T h0(u) du

and total person-time is N T, because person-time is accumulated by the whole vaccinated cohort, protected and unprotected alike. The incidence rate is therefore

IR_v = E_v / N T = (1-p) × [∫0^T h0(u) du / T] .

The unvaccinated rate is IR_u = [∫0^T h0(u) du / T]. So

IRR = IR_v/IR_u =1-p

for any T>0, and 1-IRR = p. The p we obtain is both the proportion of recipients made non-susceptible and the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated cohort. That is the usual epidemiologic definition of VE =1-IRR.

The decreasing HR(t) quoted by colleagues 1,10,11, etc. is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected, h_v(t)= -S_v'/S_v. It declines because the susceptible 1-p fraction is progressively depleted by infection while the p fraction remains and inflates the denominator S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t). That is a selection effect among survivors, not a change in the biological per-exposure risk. It is exactly why the cumulative risk ratio

RR_cum(T)=[1-S_v(T)]/[1-S0(T)]=1-p

is constant, and why in the rare-disease/short follow-up limit the conditional and marginal hazards coincide.

If 1-IRR were truly >p, VE would tend to 1 as follow-up lengthened, which would be a cumulative protection statement about the depletion of the susceptible pool, not a statement about the biological risk per exposure. The operational VE used in trials is the marginal 1-IRR, which for an all-or-nothing mechanism is the proportion protected p, i.e. the per-exposure efficacy by the standard definition. This is the same reasoning given by colleagues 13 and 14, and it is why the risk ratio and the rate ratio are both 1-p for the marginal quantity of interest.

* Vaccinated survival S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t)
* Population hazard among the whole vaccinated cohort
  h_v(t)= -S_v'/S_v = h0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]
  HR(t)=h_v/h0 = (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]
  HR(0)=1-p, monotone decreasing to 0 as susceptible vaccinated are depleted and the permanently immune fraction accumulates immortal person-time.
* Per-exposure / initial individual efficacy under the standard definition
  VE_pe =1-HR(0)=p
* Cumulative risk ratio is time constant
  R_v(t)=(1-p)[1-S0(t)], R_u(t)=1-S0(t) ⇒ RR(t)=1-p ⇒ 1-RR=p
  so risk ratio recovers the proportion protected.

Incidence density over finite follow-up T
With constant λ0
IR_v(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[pT+(1-p)λ0^{-1}(1-e^{-λ0T})]
IR_u=λ0
IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] <1-p for T>0
1-IRR(T)= pλ0T/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] >p=VE_pe
Equality only in rare-disease/short follow-up λ0T≪1. Bias grows with T, →1 as T→∞.
Hence the time-averaged hazard ratio <HR(0) so 1-IRR is upwardly biased for the instantaneous per-exposure reduction p. The protected fraction contributes person-time with zero events while the 1-p susceptible fraction is progressively depleted.

That is the argument of Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,11,12,15 in both rounds.

Minority positions
* Colleagues 13 and 14, and now Colleague 7 in round 1, claim C. correctly estimate. They define per-exposure efficacy as the marginal average hazard per randomly sampled vaccinee:
  h_v^M(t)=p·0+(1-p)h0(t)=(1-p)h0(t) ⇒ HR^M=1-p constant ⇒ IRR=1-p ⇒ 1-IRR=p.
  They argue the decreasing HR(t)=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0] is the hazard conditional on still being uninfected at t, i.e. the hazard in the residual susceptible pool after depletion. That conditional decline is a selection effect, not a change in biological per-exposure risk.
  Under that marginal definition the rate ratio is constant and 1-IRR is the population-average proportion protected.
* Colleague 7 previously argued B. underestimate on the basis of conditioning efficacy on the protected subset, essentially 100% protection for the p fraction. That is a different conditional definition and is not the usual population per-exposure definition.

Nuance noted by Colleague 6: population rate ratio =1-p is the proportion protected, while the true per-exposure reduction conditional on being susceptible is zero. So 1-IRR is an upwardly biased estimate of a genuine per-contact hazard reduction in the susceptible sub-cohort.

Current belief
Under the standard epidemiologic definition VE_pe =1-HR(0)= proportion protected p, the observed incidence rate ratio is a time average of a decreasing HR(t) and therefore IRR(T)<1-p and 1-IRR(T)>p. The bias vanishes in the rare-disease/short follow-up limit and the cumulative risk ratio, not the rate ratio, is the time-constant estimator for an all-or-nothing effect. The rate ratio is the correct constant estimator for a leaky per-exposure effect.

Unresolved definitional point remains: the “correctly estimate” camp is using the marginal average hazard per exposure definition, which makes 1-IRR =p by construction. The question as phrased in the literature conventionally targets the instantaneous/per-individual efficacy 1-HR(0), for which the rate ratio overestimates.

Survival in vaccinated: Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t). Population hazard conditional on being still uninfected:
hV(t)= -Sv′/Sv = h0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)].

IRV(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[pT+(1-p)(1-e^{-λ0T})/λ0], IRU=λ0,
IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] <1-p for T>0,
1-IRR(T)= pλ0T/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] >p, equality only λ0T≪1, →1 as T→∞.
Hence the time-averaged rate ratio is <1-p and 1-IRR is upwardly biased relative to the instantaneous per-exposure reduction p: classic depletion-of-susceptibles / immortal person-time bias. The protected p fraction contributes person-time with zero events while the 1-p susceptible fraction is progressively depleted.

Majority colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,10,11,12,15 in both rounds give the derivation above and answer A overestimate. They note risk ratio, not rate ratio, is constant estimator for all-or-nothing proportion protected; rate ratio is unbiased for leaky per-exposure.

They argue hV(t)= -Sv′/Sv is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected, a selection effect due to enrichment of immune survivors, not a change in biological per-exposure risk. S0(t)=exp[-∫h0], Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t). The population hazard among all vaccinees still uninfected is
hv(t)= -Sv′/Sv = h0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] ,
HR(t)=hv/h0=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0]. HR(0)=1-p, HR(t) monotone decreasing to 0. Per-exposure / instantaneous efficacy at entry is VE_pe=1-HR(0)=p.
Cumulative risk Rv(t)=(1-p)[1-S0(t)], Ru(t)=1-S0(t) → RRcum(t)=1-p constant, 1-RRcum=p, the proportion protected.

The observable incidence density is events / total person-time. With constant λ0
IRv(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[pT+(1-p)(1-e^{-λ0T})/λ0] , IRu=λ0
IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] <1-p for T>0,
1-IRR(T)= pλ0T/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] >p =VE_pe,
equality only λ0T≪1, and 1-IRR→1 as T→∞. The p immune fraction contributes immortal person-time with zero events while the 1-p susceptible fraction is depleted, so the time-averaged HR < HR(0).

Majority in rounds 0-1: Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,10,11,12,15 → A overestimate. They derive decreasing HR(t), constant RRcum=1-p, time-averaged IRR<1-p, so 1-IRR overestimates the instantaneous per-exposure reduction p, bias increasing with follow-up; risk ratio not rate ratio is the constant estimator for all-or-nothing.

Minority C: Colleagues 13,14 argue the marginal average hazard per randomly sampled vaccinee is hV^M(t)=p·0+(1-p)h0(t)=(1-p)h0(t), so HR^M=1-p constant, IRR=1-p, 1-IRR=p exactly, no bias. They treat the decreasing expression HR(t)=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0] as conditional on remaining uninfected, a selection effect among survivors, not a change in per-exposure risk.

Colleague 7 B: argues per-exposure efficacy should be conditional on the protected subset, ≈100% protection, so population-average 1-IRR dilutes it and underestimates.

Unresolved definition nuance: “per-exposure vaccine efficacy” = 1-HR(0)=p, the initial instantaneous hazard reduction for the cohort, versus marginal population average hazard reduction p·0+(1-p)h0. Under the standard instantaneous definition the rate ratio is upwardly biased for an all-or-nothing vaccine; under the marginal average definition 1-IRR=p is the conventional proportion protected. Current leaning is A overestimate with the classic depletion-of-susceptibles bias, with risk ratio being the constant all-or-nothing estimator and rate ratio unbiased for a leaky vaccine.

reflection_text.10:
The mixture model for an all-or-nothing vaccine remains the core: fraction p completely immune, hazard 0, fraction 1-p identical to unvaccinated with baseline hazard h0(t). 

S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t), S0=exp[-∫h0]. 
Population hazard among survivors: h_v(t)= -S_v'/S_v = h0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)], 
HR_cond(t)=h_v/h0=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0]. HR_cond(0)=1-p, monotone decreasing to 0 as susceptible vaccinees are depleted and protected accumulate immortal person-time.

Cumulative risk: V(t)=(1-p)[1-S0(t)], U(t)=1-S0(t), RR(t)=1-p constant. Hence 1-RR=p is the proportion protected, the all-or-nothing population efficacy, and equals the instantaneous per-exposure hazard ratio at t=0.

The observable incidence density ratio over follow-up T is a time-average of HR_cond:
IRR(T)=∫h_v /∫h0 = (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] <1-p for T>0, with equality only in rare-disease / short follow-up λ0T≈0. 
Hence 1-IRR(T)=pλ0T/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]]>p=1-HR(0). Person-time denominator is inflated by p fraction who never have events; average HR falls with follow-up, so 1-IRR is upwardly biased relative to the initial per-exposure hazard ratio and grows with duration, tending to 1 as T→∞.

Most colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,10,11,12,15 argue A overestimate on this depletion-of-susceptibles / immortal person-time logic. The argument is: per-exposure / entry efficacy is 1-HR(0)=p, risk ratio is constant 1-p, while rate ratio is time-averaged HR_cond <1-p so 1-IRR>p. Bias vanishes only as T→0.

Minority positions: Colleagues 13,14 claim C correctly estimate, reasoning that marginal population hazard per vaccinated person is h_v^M(t)=p·0+(1-p)h0(t)=(1-p)h0(t), so HR^M=1-p constant and IRR=1-p, 1-IRR=p. They equate per-exposure efficacy with the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated cohort, i.e. the proportion protected, and treat HR_cond(t)=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0] as a conditional hazard among survivors, a selection effect, not a change in biological per-exposure risk. Colleague 7 now makes the same marginal-hazard / selection-effect argument, moving from earlier B underestimate claim to an effectively C position.

Unresolved definitional nuance persists: whether “per-exposure vaccine efficacy” means 1-HR(0)=p, the proportion protected / initial hazard reduction, or the reduction conditional on remaining susceptible, which is 0 for the 1-p susceptible sub-cohort. Under the former, 1-IRR overestimates after any non-zero follow-up; under the latter, 1-IRR>0 overestimates an essentially zero per-exposure effect.

Current best synthesis: In standard epidemiologic practice the incidence-rate based VE is a time-averaged quantity. For an all-or-nothing mechanism it is > the true instantaneous per-exposure protection 1-HR(0)=p, i.e. it overestimates, with risk ratio being the correct constant estimator for proportion protected. The C claim is a definitional re-labeling where per-exposure VE is defined as the marginal average reduction p, in which case 1-IRR=p by construction. The disagreement is therefore definitional between conditional-on-survivor hazard vs marginal average hazard.

reflection_text.12:
The question is about the bias of 1 – incidence rate ratio for an all-or-nothing vaccine relative to the usual per-exposure / instantaneous efficacy.

Core model and consensus derivation
* Fraction p completely immune, hazard 0; fraction 1-p phenotypically unvaccinated with baseline hazard h0(t), S0(t)=exp[-∫h0].
* Vaccinated survival S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t)
* Population hazard among the whole vaccinated cohort
  h_v(t)= -S_v'/S_v = h0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]
  HR(t)=h_v/h0 = (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]
  HR(0)=1-p, monotone decreasing to 0 as susceptible vaccinated are depleted and the permanently immune fraction accumulates immortal person-time.
* Per-exposure / initial individual efficacy under the standard definition
  VE_pe =1-HR(0)=p
* Cumulative risk ratio is time constant
  R_v(t)=(1-p)[1-S0(t)], R_u(t)=1-S0(t) ⇒ RR(t)=1-p ⇒ 1-RR=p
  so risk ratio recovers the proportion protected.

Incidence density over finite follow-up T
With constant λ0
IR_v(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[pT+(1-p)λ0^{-1}(1-e^{-λ0T})]
IR_u=λ0
IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] <1-p for T>0
1-IRR(T)= pλ0T/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] >p=VE_pe
Equality only in rare-disease/short follow-up λ0T≪1. Bias grows with T, →1 as T→∞.
Hence the time-averaged hazard ratio <HR(0) so 1-IRR is upwardly biased for the instantaneous per-exposure reduction p. The protected fraction contributes person-time with zero events while the 1-p susceptible fraction is progressively depleted.

That is the argument of Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,11,12,15 in both rounds.

Minority positions
* Colleagues 13 and 14, and now Colleague 7 in round 1, claim C. correctly estimate. They define per-exposure efficacy as the marginal average hazard per randomly sampled vaccinee:
  h_v^M(t)=p·0+(1-p)h0(t)=(1-p)h0(t) ⇒ HR^M=1-p constant ⇒ IRR=1-p ⇒ 1-IRR=p.
  They argue the decreasing HR(t)=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0] is the hazard conditional on still being uninfected at t, i.e. the hazard in the residual susceptible pool after depletion. That conditional decline is a selection effect, not a change in biological per-exposure risk.
  Under that marginal definition the rate ratio is constant and 1-IRR is the population-average proportion protected.
* Colleague 7 previously argued B. underestimate on the basis of conditioning efficacy on the protected subset, essentially 100% protection for the p fraction. That is a different conditional definition and is not the usual population per-exposure definition.

Nuance noted by Colleague 6: population rate ratio =1-p is the proportion protected, while the true per-exposure reduction conditional on being susceptible is zero. So 1-IRR is an upwardly biased estimate of a genuine per-contact hazard reduction in the susceptible sub-cohort.

Current belief
Under the standard epidemiologic definition VE_pe =1-HR(0)= proportion protected p, the observed incidence rate ratio is a time average of a decreasing HR(t) and therefore IRR(T)<1-p and 1-IRR(T)>p. The bias vanishes in the rare-disease/short follow-up limit and the cumulative risk ratio, not the rate ratio, is the time-constant estimator for an all-or-nothing effect. The rate ratio is the correct constant estimator for a leaky per-exposure effect.

Unresolved definitional point remains: the “correctly estimate” camp is using the marginal average hazard per exposure definition, which makes 1-IRR =p by construction. The question as phrased in the literature conventionally targets the instantaneous/per-individual efficacy 1-HR(0), for which the rate ratio overestimates.

8.text:
A. overestimate

For an all-or-nothing product let p be the fraction completely immune, hazard 0, and 1-p be biologically unvaccinated with baseline hazard h0(t). 
With S0(t)=exp[-∫0^t h0] 

Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t)

hv(t)= -Sv'/Sv = h0(t) (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]

HR(t)=hv/h0=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]

HR(0)=1-p , HR(t) monotone decreasing to 0 as the 1-p susceptible fraction is depleted and the p immune fraction accumulates immortal person-time.

The instantaneous per-exposure / entry efficacy is

VEpe =1-HR(0)=p

and the cumulative risk ratio is constant

RRcum(t)=[1-Sv(t)]/[1-S0(t)]=1-p , 1-RRcum=p.

The observable incidence density ratio is a time average of HR(t). For constant λ0

IRR(T)=∫0^T hv /∫0^T h0 = (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]]<1-p , T>0

so

with equality only in the rare-disease/short follow-up limit λ0T≪1 and 1-IRR→1 as T→∞.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

I think the disagreement is really definitional, and once the definition of “per-exposure” is made explicit the rate ratio is not biased.

The expression
hV(t)=h0(t) (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)],   HR(t)=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]
that colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,11,12,15 are quoting is the hazard *conditional on still being uninfected at time t*, i.e.  hV(t)= -Sv′/Sv with Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t). It falls because the 1-p susceptible fraction is progressively depleted by infection while the p fraction remains and enriches the survivor pool. That is a classic selection effect among survivors, not a change in the biological risk per exposure for a vaccinee.

The marginal hazard per exposure opportunity in the vaccinated cohort is the mixture
hV^M(t)=p·0+(1-p)·h0(t)=(1-p)h0(t)
at every instant. A randomly sampled vaccinee, immune or not, faces on average (1-p) times the unvaccinated hazard per exposure. The HR for that marginal quantity is therefore constant
HR^M(t)=hV^M/h0=1-p,   VEpe=1-HR^M=p,
for all t.

The incidence rate is events per total person-time accumulated by the whole cohort, immune person-time included, exactly the denominator that corresponds to the marginal average. Hence
E[V](T)=(1-p)N∫0^T h0,
IRV = E[V]/NT = (1-p)∫0^T h0/T,
IRU = ∫0^T h0/T,
so IRR=IRV/IRU=1-p and 1-IRR=p for any T>0. The cumulative risk ratio is the same,
RRcum(T)=[1-p+(1-p)S0]/... =1-p,
so risk and rate agree on the population-average proportion protected.

The decreasing conditional HR(t) is the hazard in the residual susceptible pool after depletion. Calling 1-HR(0)=p a “per-exposure” efficacy and then comparing it to the time-averaged rate ratio conflates a conditional survivor hazard with the unconditional average hazard per exposure opportunity. The operational VE that trials report, VE=1-IRR, is the marginal average reduction per exposure in the vaccinated population. By that standard definition, which is what colleagues 13 and 14 and 7 are using, the 1-incidence rate ratio estimates the per-exposure efficacy correctly, and equals the proportion protected p. The apparent “inflation” to 1 as T→∞ is a statement about cumulative protection due to depletion of the susceptible pool, not about the per-exposure risk.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 on the algebra of the conditional hazard. With S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t) the hazard among those still uninfected is indeed h_v(t)=h0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] and HR(t) falls from 1-p to 0 as the 1-p susceptible fraction is depleted and the p immune fraction accumulates person-time. That is a real selection effect.

Where I think the disagreement is whether that conditional, survivor-enriched hazard is what is meant by “per-exposure” vaccine efficacy. In the usual epidemiologic operational definition VE =1 - IRR is the average reduction in the rate of infection per unit exposure in the vaccinated cohort as a whole, i.e. the marginal hazard per randomly sampled vaccinee, not the hazard conditional on still being uninfected at time t.

In the mixture model a fraction p has hazard 0 for all t and a fraction 1-p has hazard h0(t). The marginal population hazard per vaccinee is therefore

h_v^M(t)=p·0+(1-p)h0(t)=(1-p)h0(t)

for every t. The marginal hazard ratio is constant HR^M(t)=1-p and the expected events in follow-up T are (1-p) times the unvaccinated expectation. With the same total person-time in numerator and denominator, IR_v/IR_u =1-p for any T, so 1-IRR=p.

The decreasing expression HR(t)=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0] is the hazard conditional on survival to t, h_v(t)= -S_v'/S_v. It declines precisely because conditioning on being still uninfected enriches the risk set with the permanently immune. That is a depletion-of-susceptibles selection phenomenon, not a change in the biological risk per exposure for a vaccinee who remains susceptible. The cumulative risk ratio is also constant at 1-p, which is why in the rare-disease/short follow-up limit the conditional and marginal quantities coincide.

In practice the quantity that is reported and used as per-exposure VE is the population-average 1-IRR. Under the conventional mixture definition of an all-or-nothing product that population average is exactly the proportion protected p, and hence 1-IRR correctly estimates the per-exposure efficacy as usually defined. The “overestimate” is the difference between the marginal average hazard per exposure and the conditional hazard among survivors, not a bias of the rate ratio for the standard marginal per-exposure effect.

public_text.7:
C. correctly estimate

I think the disagreement is really definitional, and once the definition of “per-exposure” is made explicit the rate ratio is not biased.

The expression
hV(t)=h0(t) (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)],   HR(t)=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]
that colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,11,12,15 are quoting is the hazard *conditional on still being uninfected at time t*, i.e.  hV(t)= -Sv′/Sv with Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t). It falls because the 1-p susceptible fraction is progressively depleted by infection while the p fraction remains and enriches the survivor pool. That is a classic selection effect among survivors, not a change in the biological risk per exposure for a vaccinee.

The marginal hazard per exposure opportunity in the vaccinated cohort is the mixture
hV^M(t)=p·0+(1-p)·h0(t)=(1-p)h0(t)
at every instant. A randomly sampled vaccinee, immune or not, faces on average (1-p) times the unvaccinated hazard per exposure. The HR for that marginal quantity is therefore constant
HR^M(t)=hV^M/h0=1-p,   VEpe=1-HR^M=p,
for all t.

The incidence rate is events per total person-time accumulated by the whole cohort, immune person-time included, exactly the denominator that corresponds to the marginal average. Hence
E[V](T)=(1-p)N∫0^T h0,
IRV = E[V]/NT = (1-p)∫0^T h0/T,
IRU = ∫0^T h0/T,
so IRR=IRV/IRU=1-p and 1-IRR=p for any T>0. The cumulative risk ratio is the same,
RRcum(T)=[1-p+(1-p)S0]/... =1-p,
so risk and rate agree on the population-average proportion protected.

The decreasing conditional HR(t) is the hazard in the residual susceptible pool after depletion. Calling 1-HR(0)=p a “per-exposure” efficacy and then comparing it to the time-averaged rate ratio conflates a conditional survivor hazard with the unconditional average hazard per exposure opportunity. The operational VE that trials report, VE=1-IRR, is the marginal average reduction per exposure in the vaccinated population. By that standard definition, which is what colleagues 13 and 14 and 7 are using, the 1-incidence rate ratio estimates the per-exposure efficacy correctly, and equals the proportion protected p. The apparent “inflation” to 1 as T→∞ is a statement about cumulative protection due to depletion of the susceptible pool, not about the per-exposure risk.
public_text.14:
I agree with Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 on the algebra of the conditional hazard. With S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t) the hazard among those still uninfected is indeed h_v(t)=h0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] and HR(t) falls from 1-p to 0 as the 1-p susceptible fraction is depleted and the p immune fraction accumulates person-time. That is a real selection effect.

Where I think the disagreement is whether that conditional, survivor-enriched hazard is what is meant by “per-exposure” vaccine efficacy. In the usual epidemiologic operational definition VE =1 - IRR is the average reduction in the rate of infection per unit exposure in the vaccinated cohort as a whole, i.e. the marginal hazard per randomly sampled vaccinee, not the hazard conditional on still being uninfected at time t.

In the mixture model a fraction p has hazard 0 for all t and a fraction 1-p has hazard h0(t). The marginal population hazard per vaccinee is therefore

h_v^M(t)=p·0+(1-p)h0(t)=(1-p)h0(t)

for every t. The marginal hazard ratio is constant HR^M(t)=1-p and the expected events in follow-up T are (1-p) times the unvaccinated expectation. With the same total person-time in numerator and denominator, IR_v/IR_u =1-p for any T, so 1-IRR=p.

The decreasing expression HR(t)=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0] is the hazard conditional on survival to t, h_v(t)= -S_v'/S_v. It declines precisely because conditioning on being still uninfected enriches the risk set with the permanently immune. That is a depletion-of-susceptibles selection phenomenon, not a change in the biological risk per exposure for a vaccinee who remains susceptible. The cumulative risk ratio is also constant at 1-p, which is why in the rare-disease/short follow-up limit the conditional and marginal quantities coincide.

In practice the quantity that is reported and used as per-exposure VE is the population-average 1-IRR. Under the conventional mixture definition of an all-or-nothing product that population average is exactly the proportion protected p, and hence 1-IRR correctly estimates the per-exposure efficacy as usually defined. The “overestimate” is the difference between the marginal average hazard per exposure and the conditional hazard among survivors, not a bias of the rate ratio for the standard marginal per-exposure effect.

The core mixture model for an all-or-nothing vaccine is persistent: fraction p completely immune hazard 0, fraction 1-p identical to unvaccinated with baseline hazard h0(t), S0=exp[-∫h0], Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t). 

Conditional on still being uninfected the population hazard is hv(t)= -Sv′/Sv = h0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)], HR_cond(t)=hv/h0=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0]. HR_cond(0)=1-p, monotone decreasing to 0 as susceptible vaccinees are depleted and protected accumulate immortal person-time. Cumulative risk V(t)=(1-p)[1-S0(t)], U(t)=1-S0(t), RR(t)=1-p constant, so 1-RR=p is the proportion protected and equals instantaneous per-exposure hazard ratio at entry 1-HR_cond(0).

Observable incidence density ratio over follow-up T is a time average of HR_cond:
IRR(T)=∫hv/∫h0 = (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] <1-p for T>0 with equality only λ0T≈0. Hence 1-IRR(T)=pλ0T/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] >p =1-HR(0). Person-time denominator is inflated by p fraction who never have events; average HR falls with follow-up, so 1-IRR is upwardly biased relative to initial per-exposure hazard ratio and grows with duration, →1 as T→∞.

Most colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,10,11,12,15 argue A overestimate on depletion-of-susceptibles / immortal person-time logic. Colleague 7 moved from earlier B underestimate to effectively C position in round 2.

Minority positions: Colleagues 13,14 and now 7 claim C correctly estimate, reasoning that marginal population hazard per vaccinated person is hv^M(t)=p·0+(1-p)h0(t)=(1-p)h0(t), so HR^M=1-p constant and IRR=1-p, 1-IRR=p. They equate per-exposure VE with the average reduction in risk per exposure in the vaccinated cohort, i.e. the proportion protected, and treat HR_cond(t) as a conditional hazard among survivors, a selection effect, not a change in biological per-exposure risk.

Unresolved definitional nuance persists: whether “per-exposure vaccine efficacy” means 1-HR_cond(0)=p, the proportion protected / initial hazard reduction, or the reduction conditional on remaining susceptible which is 0 for the 1-p susceptible sub-cohort. Under the former, 1-IRR overestimates after any non-zero follow-up; under the latter, 1-IRR>0 overestimates an essentially zero per-exposure effect.

Current best synthesis: In standard epidemiologic practice the incidence-rate based VE is a time-averaged quantity. For an all-or-nothing mechanism it is > the true instantaneous per-exposure protection 1-HR(0)=p, i.e. it overestimates, with risk ratio being the correct constant estimator for proportion protected. The C claim is a definitional re-labelling where per-exposure VE is defined as the marginal average reduction p, in which case 1-IRR=p by construction. PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the algebra everyone has written down for the conditional hazard among those still uninfected.

S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t),  h_v(t)= -S_v'/S_v = h0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)],
HR(t)=h_v/h0=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)], HR(0)=1-p and HR(t)↓0.
That is correct and it is a selection/depletion effect: the 1-p biologically unprotected fraction is progressively removed by infection while the p permanently immune fraction accumulates immortal person-time in S_v(t). In the rare-disease/short follow-up limit the depletion is negligible and the conditional and marginal quantities coincide, which is why the expressions are often quoted.

The question is what is meant by “per-exposure vaccine efficacy”. Operationally VE=1-IRR is the average reduction in the rate of infection per unit exposure in the vaccinated cohort as a whole. That is a marginal, population-average quantity.

In the mixture model a fraction p has hazard 0 for all t and a fraction 1-p has hazard h0(t). The marginal hazard per randomly sampled vaccinee is

h_v^M(t)=p·0+(1-p)h0(t)=(1-p)h0(t),

so the marginal hazard ratio is constant

HR^M(t)=h_v^M/h0=1-p,   VE_pe=1-HR^M=p,

for every t. Expected events in follow-up T are (1-p) times the unvaccinated expectation and total person-time is accumulated by the whole vaccinated cohort, protected and unprotected alike. Hence

IR_v/IR_u = (1-p),   1-IRR=p,

and

RR_cum(T)=[1-S_v(T)]/[1-S0(T)]=1-p.

The decreasing expression HR(t)=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0] is h_v(t)= -S_v'/S_v conditional on still being uninfected at t. It declines precisely because conditioning on survival enriches the risk set with the permanently immune. That is a survivor selection phenomenon, not a change in the biological risk per exposure for a vaccinee who remains susceptible.

The conventional epidemiologic per-exposure VE is the population-average reduction per exposure opportunity, i.e. the marginal hazard ratio. Under that standard definition the 1-incidence rate ratio estimates the proportion protected p without systematic bias. The “overestimate” is the difference between the marginal average hazard per exposure and the conditional hazard among survivors, h_v(t)= -S_v'/S_v. If per-exposure is defined as the instantaneous conditional hazard 1-HR(0), then the rate ratio is a time average and differs, but that is a definitional re-labelling rather than a bias of 1-IRR for the marginal average effect that trials actually report.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: The algebra that everyone has written down for the conditional hazard is correct and it is worth keeping on the table.

S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S_0(t), 
h_v^c(t)= -S_v′/S_v = h_0(t)(1-p)S_0(t)/[p+(1-p)S_0(t)],
HR^c(t)= (1-p)S_0(t)/[p+(1-p)S_0(t)],

HR^c(0)=1-p and HR^c(t) ↓ 0 as the 1-p susceptible fraction is depleted and the p immune fraction builds up immortal person-time in the denominator. That decline is a selection / depletion effect among survivors, not a biological change in the risk per exposure for an individual who remains susceptible.

Per-exposure vaccine efficacy as it is operationally used is the average reduction in the rate of infection per unit exposure opportunity in a randomly sampled vaccinee, i.e. the marginal population-average hazard. In the mixture model an all-or-nothing product is

* fraction p : hazard 0 for all t
* fraction 1-p : hazard h_0(t) identical to unvaccinated

so the marginal hazard per vaccinee is

h_v^M(t)= p·0 + (1-p) h_0(t) = (1-p) h_0(t)

at every instant. The marginal hazard ratio is therefore constant

HR^M(t)= h_v^M/h_0 = 1-p,   VE_pe =1-HR^M = p

for all t. Expected events in follow-up T are (1-p) times the unvaccinated expectation and the incidence rate that trials report is events per total person-time accumulated by the whole vaccinated cohort, protected and unprotected alike. With the same total person-time in numerator and denominator

IR_v / IR_u = (1-p),   1-IRR = p,

and the cumulative risk ratio is also constant

RR_cum(T)=[1-S_v(T)]/[1-S_0(T)] =1-p.

The decreasing quantity HR^c(t)= (1-p)S_0/[p+(1-p)S_0] is the hazard conditional on still being uninfected at time t, h_v^c(t)= -S_v′/S_v. It declines precisely because conditioning on survival enriches the risk set with the permanently immune. That is the classic survivor enrichment, not a change in the biological per-exposure risk for a vaccinee who remains susceptible.

In ordinary epidemiologic practice VE ≡ 1-IRR is defined as that population-average reduction per exposure opportunity. By that standard definition, which is the one used in trial reporting, the marginal average for an all-or-nothing mechanism is exactly the proportion protected p, and 1-IRR estimates it. The statement that 1-IRR > p for long follow-up is a statement about cumulative protection via depletion of susceptibles and about the difference between the marginal average hazard and the conditional-on-survival hazard h_v^c(t). It is not a bias of the rate ratio for the marginal per-exposure effect that VE is conventionally taken to mean.

In the rare-disease / short follow-up limit λ_0T≪1 the conditional and marginal quantities coincide and that is the usual operating regime in which VE =1-IRR is interpreted. Under the conventional marginal definition of per-exposure efficacy the rate ratio therefore correctly estimates the per-exposure efficacy, i.e. the proportion protected p, for an all-or-nothing vaccine.

HR(t)=h v/h0=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)],

HR(0)=1-p and HR(t) is monotone decreasing to 0. The 1-p susceptible vaccinated are progressively depleted by infection while the p fraction accumulates immortal person-time.

The instantaneous, entry per-exposure efficacy is the initial hazard ratio

VEpe =1-HR(0)=p,

and on the cumulative risk scale

R v(t)=(1-p)[1-S0(t)], R u(t)=1-S0(t) ⇒ RRcum(t)=1-p,
1-RRcum=p is constant.

The incidence density that is reported is the time average of HR(t). With constant λ0

IR v(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[pT+(1-p)(1-e^{-λ0T})/λ0], IR u=λ0

IRR(T)= (1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] <1-p , T>0
IRR→1-p as T→0 and IRR→0 as T→∞.

Hence

1-IRR(T)= pλ0T/[pλ0T+(1-p)[1-e^{-λ0T}]] > p =1-HR(0),

with equality only in the rare disease/short follow-up limit λ0T≪1 and 1-IRR(T)→1 as T→∞.

I think the algebra everyone has written down for the conditional hazard is correct, but it is being read as the per-exposure quantity when it is in fact the hazard conditional on still being uninfected at time t.

With an all-or-nothing product we have a mixture at entry:
* fraction p: hazard 0 for all t
* fraction 1-p: hazard h0(t) identical to unvaccinated

The survival in the vaccinated arm is Sv(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t) and the hazard among those who remain uninfected is indeed
hv(t) = -Sv′/Sv = h0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)],
HR(t)= (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)] ↓ 0.

That decline is a classic survivor selection / depletion effect. The risk set Sv(t) is progressively enriched with the permanently immune p fraction as the 1-p susceptible fraction is removed by infection. HR(t) is therefore the hazard conditional on survival to t, not the biological risk per exposure for a randomly sampled vaccinee.

Per-exposure efficacy in the usual epidemiologic operational sense is the average reduction in the rate of infection per unit exposure opportunity in the vaccinated cohort as a whole. The marginal population hazard per randomly sampled vaccinee is the mixture
hV^M(t)=p·0+(1-p)h0(t)=(1-p)h0(t)
at every instant. Hence the marginal hazard ratio is constant
HR^M(t)=hV^M/h0=1-p
and VEpe=1-HR^M=p for all t.

The incidence rate that trials report is events divided by total person-time accumulated by the whole vaccinated cohort, immune person-time included. That is precisely the marginal average. Expected events in follow-up T are (1-p)N∫0^T h0, total person-time is NT, so

IRv/IRu = (1-p)∫0^T h0 /T ÷ ∫0^T h0 /T =1-p

and 1-IRR=p. The cumulative risk ratio is also [1-Sv]/[1-S0]=1-p, so risk and rate agree on the population-average proportion protected.

Calling 1-HR(0)=p the “per-exposure” efficacy and then comparing it to the time-averaged rate ratio conflates a conditional-on-still-uninfected hazard with the unconditional average hazard per exposure opportunity. The decreasing conditional HR(t) is the hazard in the residual susceptible pool after depletion, not a change in the biological per-exposure risk for a susceptible individual.

Under the conventional marginal definition VE≡1-IRR, which is the average reduction per exposure opportunity in the vaccinated population, the 1-incidence rate ratio estimates the per-exposure efficacy correctly and equals the proportion protected p. The apparent inflation of 1-IRR to 1 as T→∞ is a statement about cumulative protection via eventual depletion of the susceptible pool, not about a change in the per-exposure risk. In the rare-disease/short follow-up limit where most trials operate the conditional and marginal quantities coincide anyway, making the practical bias negligible.

So for the standard population-average definition of per-exposure VE, the rate ratio is correctly estimating it, i.e. C.

I agree with the algebra everyone has written down for the conditional hazard among those still uninfected.

S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t),  h_v(t)= -S_v'/S_v = h0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)],
HR(t)=h_v/h0=(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)], HR(0)=1-p and HR(t)↓0.
That is correct and it is a selection/depletion effect: the 1-p biologically unprotected fraction is progressively removed by infection while the p permanently immune fraction accumulates immortal person-time in S_v(t). In the rare-disease/short follow-up limit the depletion is negligible and the conditional and marginal quantities coincide, which is why the expressions are often quoted.

The question is what is meant by “per-exposure vaccine efficacy”. Operationally VE=1-IRR is the average reduction in the rate of infection per unit exposure in the vaccinated cohort as a whole. That is a marginal, population-average quantity.

In the mixture model a fraction p has hazard 0 for all t and a fraction 1-p has hazard h0(t). The marginal hazard per randomly sampled vaccinee is

h_v^M(t)=p·0+(1-p)h0(t)=(1-p)h0(t),

so the marginal hazard ratio is constant

HR^M(t)=h_v^M/h0=1-p,   VE_pe=1-HR^M=p,

for every t. Expected events in follow-up T are (1-p) times the unvaccinated expectation and total person-time is accumulated by the whole vaccinated cohort, protected and unprotected alike. Hence

IR_v/IR_u = (1-p),   1-IRR=p,

and

RR_cum(T)=[1-S_v(T)]/[1-S0(T)]=1-p.

The decreasing expression HR(t)=(1-p)S0/[p+(1-p)S0] is h_v(t)= -S_v'/S_v conditional on still being uninfected at t. It declines precisely because conditioning on survival enriches the risk set with the permanently immune. That is a survivor selection phenomenon, not a change in the biological risk per exposure for a vaccinee who remains susceptible.

The conventional epidemiologic per-exposure VE is the population-average reduction per exposure opportunity, i.e. the marginal hazard ratio. Under that standard definition the 1-incidence rate ratio estimates the proportion protected p without systematic bias. The “overestimate” is the difference between the marginal average hazard per exposure and the conditional hazard among survivors, h_v(t)= -S_v'/S_v. If per-exposure is defined as the instantaneous conditional hazard 1-HR(0), then the rate ratio is a time average and differs, but that is a definitional re-labelling rather than a bias of 1-IRR for the marginal average effect that trials actually report.

The algebra that everyone has written down for the conditional hazard is correct and it is worth keeping on the table.

S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S_0(t), 
h_v^c(t)= -S_v′/S_v = h_0(t)(1-p)S_0(t)/[p+(1-p)S_0(t)],
HR^c(t)= (1-p)S_0(t)/[p+(1-p)S_0(t)],

HR^c(0)=1-p and HR^c(t) ↓ 0 as the 1-p susceptible fraction is depleted and the p immune fraction builds up immortal person-time in the denominator. That decline is a selection / depletion effect among survivors, not a biological change in the risk per exposure for an individual who remains susceptible.

Per-exposure vaccine efficacy as it is operationally used is the average reduction in the rate of infection per unit exposure opportunity in a randomly sampled vaccinee, i.e. the marginal population-average hazard. In the mixture model an all-or-nothing product is

* fraction p : hazard 0 for all t
* fraction 1-p : hazard h_0(t) identical to unvaccinated

so the marginal hazard per vaccinee is

h_v^M(t)= p·0 + (1-p) h_0(t) = (1-p) h_0(t)

at every instant. The marginal hazard ratio is therefore constant

HR^M(t)= h_v^M/h_0 = 1-p,   VE_pe =1-HR^M = p

for all t. Expected events in follow-up T are (1-p) times the unvaccinated expectation and the incidence rate that trials report is events per total person-time accumulated by the whole vaccinated cohort, protected and unprotected alike. With the same total person-time in numerator and denominator

IR_v / IR_u = (1-p),   1-IRR = p,

and the cumulative risk ratio is also constant

RR_cum(T)=[1-S_v(T)]/[1-S_0(T)] =1-p.

The decreasing quantity HR^c(t)= (1-p)S_0/[p+(1-p)S_0] is the hazard conditional on still being uninfected at time t, h_v^c(t)= -S_v′/S_v. It declines precisely because conditioning on survival enriches the risk set with the permanently immune. That is the classic survivor enrichment, not a change in the biological per-exposure risk for a vaccinee who remains susceptible.

In ordinary epidemiologic practice VE ≡ 1-IRR is defined as that population-average reduction per exposure opportunity. By that standard definition, which is the one used in trial reporting, the marginal average for an all-or-nothing mechanism is exactly the proportion protected p, and 1-IRR estimates it. The statement that 1-IRR > p for long follow-up is a statement about cumulative protection via depletion of susceptibles and about the difference between the marginal average hazard and the conditional-on-survival hazard h_v^c(t). It is not a bias of the rate ratio for the marginal per-exposure effect that VE is conventionally taken to mean.

In the rare-disease / short follow-up limit λ_0T≪1 the conditional and marginal quantities coincide and that is the usual operating regime in which VE =1-IRR is interpreted. Under the conventional marginal definition of per-exposure efficacy the rate ratio therefore correctly estimates the per-exposure efficacy, i.e. the proportion protected p, for an all-or-nothing vaccine.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

I think the conditional/marginal distinction is the key point here and it resolves the apparent paradox.

The algebra everyone has written down for the conditional hazard among those still uninfected is correct:
S_v(t)=p+(1-p)S0(t)
h_v^c(t)= -S_v′/S_v = h0(t)(1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)]
HR^c(t)= (1-p)S0(t)/[p+(1-p)S0(t)],  HR^c(0)=1-p →0.

That decline is real, but it is a survivor-enrichment / depletion-of-susceptibles effect. HR^c(t) is the hazard conditional on remaining uninfected at time t. As the 1-p phenotypically unvaccinated fraction is progressively removed, the risk set S_v(t) becomes enriched with the p permanently immune fraction that contributes immortal person-time with zero events. That is selection among survivors, not a biological change in the risk per exposure for a person who remains susceptible.

Per-exposure vaccine efficacy as it is operationally used in trials is the average reduction in the rate of infection per unit exposure opportunity in a randomly sampled vaccinee, i.e. the marginal population-average hazard. In the all-or-nothing mixture

* fraction p : hazard 0 for all t
* fraction 1-p : hazard h0(t)

the marginal hazard per vaccinee is
h_v^M(t)=p·0+(1-p)h0(t)=(1-p)h0(t)
at every instant. Hence the marginal hazard ratio is constant

HR^M(t)=h_v^M/h0=1-p
VE_pe=1-HR^M=p

for all t. Expected events in follow-up T are (1-p) times the unvaccinated expectation and total person-time is accumulated by the whole vaccinated cohort, protected and unprotected alike. So

IR_v/IR_u =1-p ,   1-IRR=p

and the cumulative risk ratio is also [1-S_v]/[1-S0]=1-p.

The decreasing HR^c(t) is h_v^c(t)= -S_v′/S_v conditional on still being uninfected. It declines precisely because conditioning on survival enriches the risk set with the permanently immune. That is not the biological per-exposure risk for a vaccinee who remains susceptible; it is the hazard in the residual susceptible pool after depletion.

By the conventional epidemiologic definition VE≡1-IRR is that population-average reduction per exposure opportunity. Under that standard definition the rate ratio estimates the proportion protected p without systematic bias. The time-averaged inequality 1-IRR(T)>p is a statement about the difference between the marginal average hazard and the conditional-on-survival hazard h_v^c(t), and about cumulative protection via depletion of susceptibles with long follow-up. In the rare-disease/short follow-up regime where trials operate the conditional and marginal quantities coincide anyway, making the practical bias negligible.

So with the standard marginal definition of per-exposure efficacy the 1-incidence rate ratio correctly estimates it, i.e. the proportion protected p.
